title: Redwood Optimize Walkthrough - batching & caching recommendations
next_steps: Jordan to send Optimize config template and cost model spreadsheet
Priya to run a 48h perf benchmark on their sample traffic and share results
Customer to provide sample prefix distribution CSV and expected P95 latency SLO
action_items: Jordan Lee - Send pricing + Optimize template - 2025-02-17
Priya Sharma - Run 48h batching & cache benchmark using their sample - 2025-02-20
Maya Chen - Share prefix distribution and failure cases - 2025-02-16
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked StellarPay through Redwood Optimize features focused on batching and prefix/KV caching. Covered trade-offs (latency vs. cost), recommended param ranges for batch windows and cache TTLs, and shared unit economics models. Agreed next steps: benchmark run, share prefix distribution, and send cost model spreadsheet.
topics: Batching parameters (batch window, max batch size)
Cache hit-rate modeling and cost impact
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-14
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Sharma (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood SE), Evan Torres (CTO - StellarPay), Maya Chen (ML Eng), Liam O'Neill (VP Product)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I think we have about 50 minutes, we want to run through Redwood Optimize, specifically batching and caching recommendations for the payment flows you mentioned in the precall.
[00:12] Evan Torres: Yep, thanks Jordan. Quick note — we care about P95 latency under 400ms for the auth flow, and cost per 1M tokens is obviously a factor.
[00:25] Priya Sharma: Great. I'll start with a quick slide set and then jump into the console demo showing how Optimize suggests batching windows and prefix / K-V cache configs. Excuse my accent on the demo — my screen's a bit laggy.
[00:40] Carlos Mendes: FYI we uploaded the sample traffic and prefix distribution you sent, so we can show the simulated modeling in the console.
[00:48] Maya Chen: Perfect, that sample is the one with a heavy tail — small prefixes for auth strings and a few very common merchant prompts.
[00:57] Priya Sharma: Exactly. Okay first slide — Optimize looks at three vectors: request shape (seq length, tokens), temporal locality (prefix repeat rate), and hardware profile. Our recommendations are in two buckets: batching (how many requests to combine & max wait) and caching (prefix vs. KV cache).
[01:20] Liam O'Neill: When you say prefix cache, you mean storing the left context token keys, the KV-thing?
[01:27] Priya Sharma: Yeah, we sometimes call it prefix/KV cache — it's the KV cache entries keyed by prefix hash. That lets us resume generation much faster for repeated prefixes; good for sessions or templated prompts.
[01:40] Evan Torres: Does that change model quality in any way? We can't have mismatched context.
[01:45] Priya Sharma: Good question — no change to model params; it's a performance optimization. You need to be careful with prompt mutations — if the prefix is slightly changed (e.g., merchant name inserted), hit rates fall. We showed a heuristic for fuzzy-prefix matching, but it has consistency tradeoffs.
[02:05] Jordan Lee: And on the cost model side, our spreadsheet computes effective tokens served vs tokens avoided. For example, with a 65% cache hit rate on a 30-token prefix, you might avoid ~19 tokens per request, which at your committed hosted rates is a substantial savings.
[02:22] Maya Chen: Can you show the math? We're trying to map to our monthly usage — mostly short prompts but high QPS.
[02:30] Priya Sharma: Sure — demoing the console now: (screen share) — here's the Optimize tab, we uploaded their prefix distribution. The recommendation engine suggests a 10-25ms batch window for your QPS and a max_batch_size of 16 for our dedicated GPUs; for hosted it nudges lower if you prefer lower warmup.
[02:50] [02:51] Priya Sharma: Note: the transcribed slide shows "max batch site" sometimes in the slide notes, ignore that, it's a small OCR glitch.
[03:00] Jordan Lee: Also important — batching has a tail latency amplification. If you increase the batch window you lower cost per token but you add wait time. The console shows simulated P50/P95 for each setting.
[03:15] Evan Torres: In the simulation we see P95 jumps from 320ms to 480ms with a 40ms batch window. That's too high for auth.
[03:25] Priya Sharma: Right — so for auth we recommended a smaller batch window (5-15ms) and rely on prefix caching for repeated sessions. For lower-SLO flows (summaries, longer reads) you can use larger window.
[03:40] Maya Chen: What about KV cache TTL and eviction? We have a lot of merchants and can't keep everything forever.
[03:47] Priya Sharma: TTL is settable per-policy. Typical pattern: short TTL (5-20 minutes) for high QPS ephemeral prefixes, and a longer TTL for known high-value merchant prompts. Eviction uses LRU per-shard. We also support adaptive eviction based on hit-rate and cost model — if a prefix's hit-rate falls below threshold we drop it.
[04:10] Liam O'Neill: How do you measure prefix hit-rate? Is it exact string matching?
[04:15] Priya Sharma: By default exact match on normalized prefix (whitespace normalized, lowercased optionally). We also offer fuzzy-prefix with a similarity threshold; that can increase hits but introduce risk if not tuned. The console visualizes the hit-rate distribution from sample traffic.
[04:32] [04:33] Carlos Mendes: Jumping into the benchmark tab — here's a mock run we did with their sample. With caching enabled and 60% hit-rate, cost per 1M tokens dropped by ~28% in the simulation. Without caching and with a 20ms batch window, cost was X (we show numbers in the spreadsheet).
[04:58] Evan Torres: X not a number? The sheet in the chat had numbers — could you post the sheet after?
[05:05] Jordan Lee: We'll send the export — apologies the server hiccup cut off one cell in the demo.
[05:10] Priya Sharma: Continuing — important nuance: when you enable prefix caching it can reduce KV cache pressure but increase memory footprint. On dedicated hosts you can adjust per-pool cache memory. For hosted customers we usually recommend starting with a small TTL and measuring.
[05:30] Maya Chen: Are there any consistency guarantees if we have cross-region routing? Our main app is multi-region.
[05:37] Priya Sharma: We don't replicate KV cache across regions for latency reasons — we route to the region where cache keys live. For global failover we have fallback policies: route to nearest region without cache or use a smaller compatible model. That has cost/latency tradeoffs which Optimize models for.
[05:55] Liam O'Neill: Any SSO or compliance concerns? Our security team will ask about KMS and audit logs.
[06:02] Jordan Lee: Yes we integrate with customer KMS for Private deployments and support BYOK for Dedicated. Audit logs for cache evictions and config changes are captured in the Console's audit trail and exported to S3 or SIEM. We'll send the SOC2 docs in the follow-up.
[06:20] Evan Torres: Good. Back to the cost math — show me a worked example for our auth path: average seq len 80 tokens, prefix is 20 tokens repeatable 50% of calls, QPS 200.
[06:32] Priya Sharma: Sure. Rough calc: tokens_per_req = 80. If prefix=20 and 50% hit, average tokens avoided = 0.5*20 = 10 tokens. Effective tokens served = 80 - 10 = 70. With your hosted rate of $0.5 per 1k tokens (example) that becomes savings of approx $5 per million tokens. The spreadsheet will compute across monthly QPS.
[07:00] Maya Chen: You said 0.5 per 1k tokens — that's our public benchmark earlier, but committed rates might be lower for dedicated.
[07:08] Jordan Lee: Exactly — dedicated reserved capacity changes the math: CPU/GPU amortization and longer batch sizes can reduce per-token cost but increases fixed monthly commitment. Optimize's model shows both marginal and amortized cost lines.
[07:22] [07:22] Priya Sharma: Also note we model cold cache misses on start of day and TTL churn; the hit-rate you see in console is steady-state simulation. We include warm-up factor to account for traffic ramps.
[07:36] Evan Torres: Regarding batching window — you said 10-25ms recommended. How deterministic is that?
[07:42] Priya Sharma: It's a recommendation based on observed interarrival times. For your 200 QPS auth flow we saw median inter-arrival per instance ~12ms, so a 10-20ms window gives decent batching without pushing P95 too much. We usually recommend starting at half the recommended window and ramping.
[07:58] Liam O'Neill: Can we run a POC for 48 hours to capture real hit rates?
[08:03] Jordan Lee: Absolutely — that's on the next steps. Priya will run a 48h test in a dedicated sandbox using your sample.
[08:10] [08:11] Maya Chen: A couple of edge cases — what about prompt templating where we inject time or user IDs in the prompt? That will defeat exact prefix hits.
[08:19] Priya Sharma: Correct — for templated prompts we recommend normalizing the prefix (replace time/user-id tokens with placeholders) before hashing for cache keys. Optimize can ingest tokenization rules to canonicalize prefixes. That increases hit-rate without changing model output.
[08:33] Jordan Lee: Also we support partial-prefix caching for repeated start tokens; this is sometimes called "prefix truncation" in the console. It can help when the variation is at end of prefix.
[08:45] Evan Torres: Does that add risk of leaking sensitive merchant PII?
[08:49] Priya Sharma: The cache keys are hashed and encrypted at rest; you can also opt out of storing specific prefixes via a denylist. For Private deployment we can run with zero persist policy if needed.
[09:03] Carlos Mendes: Demoing the Console's cost model now — here's the slider for hit-rate, batch window, and TTL. When I slide hit-rate from 30% to 70% you can see cost per million tokens fall and ROI increases. There's also a dashboard that shows expected latency impact and risk band.
[09:25] [09:26] Maya Chen: About that ROI number — does it include the overhead of cache memory (additional infra cost) and increased memory ops?
[09:32] Carlos Mendes: Yes, our back of the envelope includes memory cost per GB per month allocated to cache and the additional egress if cross-region misses occur. It also models request batching CPU overhead. The spreadsheet we shared separates infra and token charge lines.
[09:50] Liam O'Neill: If we wanted to try aggressive caching with fuzzy matching, what's the rollback plan if quality drops?
[09:57] Priya Sharma: Canary rollout in the Console. You can enable fuzzy matching for X% of traffic. We recommend tying quality checks into your eval set — Redwood can run diff evals on a holdout prompt set and raise alerts if quality diverges beyond threshold.
[10:14] Evan Torres: That eval hook — is it out-of-box or needs custom work?
[10:18] Priya Sharma: It's built-in in Optimize. You upload an eval prompt set, define acceptable regression e.g., <2% score delta, and the rollout will auto-pause and rollback if triggered.
[10:29] [10:30] Jordan Lee: Quick note — sometimes transcripts show product as "Redwood Optimiser" in the logs — that's just a spelling variant in the demo notes.
[10:37] Maya Chen: Great. On perf — what about cold-starts for rare prefixes? We have many one-off merchant strings.
[10:44] Priya Sharma: Cold starts are inevitable. We suggest two mitigations: 1) canonicalize and redact low-value tokens so similar prefixes cluster; 2) use small batch window for rare flows to avoid adding latency. If many rare prefixes exist, caching doesn't help much and batching is primary lever.
[11:03] Evan Torres: Any limits on number of cached entries? We might have millions of unique prefixes.
[11:09] Priya Sharma: We shard cache and you can configure per-shard memory and total entry cap. For millions of keys we recommend a longer-tail eviction policy and a tiered cache (hot vs. warm). We'll include recommended parameters in the template we send.
[11:26] Liam O'Neill: What about model quantization and its effect on latency/cost used in the Optimize recommendations?
[11:32] Carlos Mendes: Optimize factors quantization profiles per model. Quantized variants reduce memory and increase throughput; the console will recommend quantized models when the quality delta is within your tolerance and the cost savings are material.
[11:48] Maya Chen: If we move to Dedicated, will we be able to tune batching more aggressively?
[11:53] Jordan Lee: Yes — Dedicated lets you tune batch_max_size higher and we can allocate more memory to cache. But remember committed spend increases. The cost model shows amortized cost per token vs on-demand hosted cost.
[12:05] [12:06] Priya Sharma: Quick demo of a real run in the sandbox: here's 24h trace — you can see hit-rate by hour, and TTL churn during peak hours caused a drop from 62% to 48% which impacted cost. That helped us identify a TTL too low for a particular merchant cluster.
[12:26] Evan Torres: Can we set per-prefix TTLs programmatically?
[12:30] Priya Sharma: Yep — via API you can set TTL rules or use the Console matcher. You can also tag prefixes and set group TTLs.
[12:38] Maya Chen: On security — can we encrypt the cache in transit between Redwood and customer VPC?
[12:43] Jordan Lee: Yes TLS in transit; for Private deployments we support colocated cache that never leaves your network. For Dedicated we can enable VPC peering and private subnets.
[12:55] Liam O'Neill: Anything else that typically surprises customers?
[12:59] Priya Sharma: The common surprise is that small prompt normalization rules can dramatically improve hit-rate; investing a little effort in canonicalization often beats more aggressive infra changes.
[13:12] Evan Torres: That makes sense. Can you share a canonicalization cookbook?
[13:15] Jordan Lee: Yes, we'll include a short cookbook in the follow-up along with the sample config and the cost spreadsheet.
[13:24] [13:25] Carlos Mendes: One more demo note — in the benchmark we also show tail-latency percentiles per batch size. For your SLOs we recommended staying under max_batch_size 16 and batch window under 20ms for auth.
[13:40] Maya Chen: Are there any SDK changes on our side to enable prefix hashing?
[13:44] Priya Sharma: Minimal — we provide a client lib that can send normalized prefix meta and a cache key. If you prefer zero client changes we can do a proxy-level normalization, but client-level gives better accuracy.
[13:58] Evan Torres: Anything about rollout velocity? We want to be conservative.
[14:02] Priya Sharma: Canary 5-10% with automated eval checks is the safe path. The Console supports phased rollouts and will auto rollback if quality drops.
[14:12] Jordan Lee: Ok we're getting near the end — quick recap and next steps.
[14:16] Jordan Lee: Recap: 1) For auth: small batch window (5-15ms), max_batch_size <= 16, prefix caching with short TTL and canonicalization. 2) For lower-SLO flows: larger batch window 25-50ms, higher max_batch_size, longer TTL. 3) Run 48h benchmark, share prefix distribution, Redwood sends cost spreadsheet + canonicalization cookbook + SOC2 docs.
[14:44] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Thanks.
[14:47] Evan Torres: Thanks everyone.
[14:49] Liam O'Neill: We'll watch for the spreadsheet.
[14:51] Jordan Lee: I'll follow up with the items; Priya will run the sandbox run.
[14:55] Carlos Mendes: I'll include the sandbox run ID and the raw logs for their analysis.
[14:59] Jordan Lee: Thanks all, we'll follow up by Tuesday with the materials.
[15:02] [END]
